pl-l3d7c2-d1e114.summary: States the second opinion's view of predestination: Christ is predestined as man, i.e., as subsisting of two substances, soul and flesh; as to the divine nature he is not predestined, so not insofar as he subsists in it, but insofar as he subsists in soul and flesh.
claims: Christ is predestined insofar as he subsists in soul and flesh.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e117.summary: Reports how the second opinion interprets authorities favoring the first: 'that man was assumed into singularity of person' or 'made one person with the Word' refers to human nature united to the Word in singularity of person, i.e., so that the same person that was simple remained unchanged and without increase in number, though composite. This composition differs from other men's: of three substances rather than two.
claims: Texts on the assumed man refer to human nature united in one person.
Christ's composition is of three substances, other men's of two.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e120.summary: Adds that they deny human nature is a person or Son of God; as they say God and man, Son of God and son of man, are one and the same person, so they are one and the same thing, not one and another thing.
claims: Human nature is not a person or Son of God.
God and man in Christ are not one thing and another.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e123.summary: Notes that the texts in the following chapters seem to oppose them.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e127.summary: Cites Augustine on John: the Word of God is one thing, man another; but the Word was made flesh, i.e., man; so there is not one person of the Word and another of the man, since both are Christ and one person.
claims: The Word and the man are different things but one person.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e139.summary: Cites Augustine, Ad Felicianum: the Son of God is one thing, the son of man another, but not another person.
claims: Son of God and son of man are different things but not different persons.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e148.summary: Adds: the Son of God has one thing from the Father, another from his mother.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e154.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate I: since the Son is God and man, God is one substance and man another.
claims: God and man in Christ are different substances.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e163.summary: Gives the second opinion's interpretation: 'the Word of God is one thing, man another' or 'God is one substance, man another' means Christ is of one nature as man and of another as God, and the nature by which he is man differs from that by which he is God.
claims: 'One thing and another' refers to Christ's two natures.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e166.summary: Cites John Damascene: the natures are united without conversion or alteration, neither the divine leaving its simplicity nor the human converted or destroyed, nor one composite nature made. A composite nature cannot be consubstantial with its components, as a body from four elements is none of them; if Christ were one composite nature, he would be consubstantial with neither Father nor mother, and would be called neither God nor man. 'Christ' names a person signifying two natures; we confess the same perfect God and perfect man from and in two natures.
claims: The natures are united without conversion or composition into one nature.
A composite nature would make Christ consubstantial with neither Father nor mother.
'Christ' names a person of two natures.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e179.summary: Concludes: the Son of God is said to be one thing and the son of man another because he is of one nature as Son of God and of another as son of man, not because the Son of God and man is those two diverse things, i.e., two diverse natures.
claims: The Son of God and of man is not two diverse things.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e182.summary: Confirms with Hilary, De Trinitate IX: the son of man is not one thing and the Son of God another, since the Word was made flesh; the one who is Son of God is son of man. Hilary plainly says they are not different things, which confirms this interpretation.
claims: Son of God and son of man are not different things.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e197.summary: Raises texts that may trouble the reader: 'both are Christ and one person', and Augustine, De Trinitate I: since the form of God took the form of a servant, both are God and both man, both God because of God assuming, both man because of man assumed.
claims: Augustine says both are God and both are man.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e209.summary: Adds Augustine, De dono perseverantiae: the faithful believe human nature was so exalted by the Word that the assumer and the assumed were one person in the Trinity. The inference is drawn that human nature and the Word are one person.
claims: Objection: human nature with the Word is one person.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e218.summary: Gives the second opinion's reading: 'both are Christ and one person' because one Christ and one person subsists in both; the assumed is one person with the assumer because it is joined in unity of person, so that the unity of the person remained, not that flesh and soul are God, since, as Jerome says, the Word is God, not the flesh assumed.
claims: One person subsists in both natures.
Flesh and soul are not God.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e224.summary: Adds Ambrose, De Spiritu sancto III: what assumed and what was assumed are different.
claims: The assumer and the assumed differ.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e237.summary: Introduces another text that seems strongly to oppose this opinion.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e240.summary: Cites Augustine, Contra Maximinum: Christ is one person of twofold substance, God and man, yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person, otherwise the Son of God was not whole before taking the form of a servant and grew when man was added. This seems to show the person is not made of God and man.
claims: Neither God nor man is part of Christ's person.
Otherwise the Son was incomplete before the incarnation.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e252.summary: Gives the second opinion's answer: the person does not consist of God and man as a whole of parts, since parts come together to make what was not; the divine and human natures are not united that way, for the account of this union, which is not of parts, is inexplicable.
claims: The union in Christ is not of parts forming a whole.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e255.summary: Reports another reading: some think 'God' there signifies a person, since Augustine was speaking of the three persons, none of which is a part of the Trinity, as God is not part of this person; and a person is plainly not part of a person.
claims: A person is not part of a person.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e258.summary: Concludes that the second opinion has been carefully set out and explained, and that the authorities cited for the third oppose it little or not at all; now the third must be considered.
claims: The authorities for the third opinion hardly oppose the second.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e261.summary: Explains the third opinion's reading: God was made man because he took a man; he is man because he has a man; man was made God because he was assumed by God; and man is God because the one having man is God. In 'God is man', either habitus or the person, but humanated, is predicated.
claims: On the third opinion, God is man because he has a man.
'God is man' predicates habitus or the humanated person.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e265.summary: Cites Cassiodorus as showing that the humanated person is predicated: God was made, so to speak, humanated, without ceasing to be God. 'God was made man' thus has several senses on this view, that he took human nature or began to be the humanated Word. If he began to be the humanated Word it does not follow that he began to be the Word, as one who today became a good man did not today become a man.
claims: God became humanated without ceasing to be God.
Beginning to be the humanated Word does not imply beginning to be the Word.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e274.summary: Explains the third opinion on predestination: Christ as man is predestined Son of God because it was predestined from eternity and conferred on him in time by grace that he, being man, is Son of God; this he did not always have but received in time by grace.
claims: It was conferred on Christ by grace in time that, being man, he is Son of God.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e277.summary: Cites Augustine, Ad Prosperum et Hilarium: Jesus was predestined so that he who would be son of David according to the flesh would be Son of God in power.
claims: Jesus was predestined to be Son of God in power.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e292.summary: Adds that the third opinion reads 'Christ is less than the Father as man' according to habitus, i.e., insofar as he has a man united to himself.
claims: Christ is less than the Father by habitus.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e295.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate I: God the Son is equal to the Father by nature, less by habitus; less in the form of a servant, equal in the form of God.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father by nature and less by habitus.
concepts: form of God and form of a servant

pl-l3d7c2-d1e307.summary: Notes that because the incarnation is understood by habitus, they say God was humanated, not man deified.
claims: God was humanated, not man deified.

pl-l3d7c2-d1e311.summary: Cites John Damascene: we do not say man was deified, but God was made man.
claims: We say God was made man, not man deified.

pl-l3d7c2.summary: Develops the second and third opinions. On the second, Christ is predestined as man, i.e., as subsisting in soul and flesh; texts calling the assumed man one person with the Word mean the human nature united in singularity of person; the person, though composite, stays the same, composed of three substances rather than two. They deny human nature is a person or Son of God. Augustine's 'one thing the Word, another the man' is read as signifying distinct natures, not that the Son of God and son of man are two diverse things (Damascene, Hilary). 'Both are one person' means one person subsists in both, and 'God is not part of this person' means the union is not of parts in a whole. The third opinion, little opposed by the authorities, reads 'God is man' as God having a man, predicating habitus or the 'humanated' person (Cassiodorus); Christ is predestined as man because it was conferred on him by grace in time, and is less than the Father by habitus. Hence one speaks of God made man, not man deified (Damascene).
claims: On the second opinion, Christ is predestined as subsisting in soul and flesh.
Human nature is not itself a person or the Son of God.
'One thing the Word, another the man' signifies distinct natures, not two things in Christ.
The union is not of parts forming a whole.
On the third opinion, 'God is man' means God has a man.
Christ is less than the Father by habitus.
God was made man, not man deified.
